Tay-Sachs is a genetic disorder. It is caused by the absence of a vital enzyme known as Hex-A, which is encoded by the HEXA gene. This missing enzyme causes cells to become damaged, resulting in progressive neurological disorders. The disorder can occur in different forms or types, with the most common being Infantile Tay-Sachs, Juvenile Tay-Sachs, and Late Onset Tay-Sachs (LOTS). The form or type is determined by the age of the individual when symptoms first appear. Infantile Tay-Sachs appears normal at birth and typically continues to develop like any other child for the first six months, but after this development slows, and parents may notice a reduction in vision and a prominent startle response. Children with Infantile Tay-Sachs gradually regress, losing skills one by one and eventually becoming mostly non-responsive to their environment. Juvenile Tay-Sachs has early symptoms including lack of coordination or clumsiness and muscle weakness, while Late Onset Tay-Sachs (LOTS) has early symptoms including clumsiness and muscle weakness in the legs, and mental health symptoms such as bi-polar or psychotic episodes.
